The library gives you two general sorts.
makes no promise about elements that compare equal;
promises that equivalent elements keep the order they arrived in. Both take a comparator, a function answering whether one element must come strictly before another, and that comparator has to be a
: irreflexive, an element is never less than itself; asymmetric, if a is less than b then b is never less than a; and transitive for both "less than" and "equivalent".

The problem is ordering elements by a rule the library cannot know in advance, while still getting a guaranteed cost and a defined answer for ties. A comparator lets you sort a job queue by priority and then by deadline, or detections by label and then confidence, without writing a sorting algorithm yourself; getting the tie-breaking wrong, not the sort, is where most of these solutions actually fail.

Two sorts are worth knowing from the inside.

splits the range in half, sorts each half, and merges the two sorted halves by taking the smaller front element each time. Halving gives log₂ n levels, and the merges on one level touch all n elements, so it makes O(n log n) comparisons on every input. The merge needs a buffer, O(n) extra space. It is stable if the merge takes from the left half when the two front elements are equivalent.

picks a pivot, partitions the range into the elements less than the pivot and the rest, and sorts both parts. It works in place and makes O(n log n) comparisons on average. A bad pivot on every step makes it O(n²), and the textbook version that takes the last element as its pivot does exactly that on input that is already sorted, recursing n levels deep. It isn't stable, because partitioning swaps elements across long distances.
